A sheet of paper is a mat of plant fibres, mostly air, held together by water.
To make it by hand, you soak and beat bark until the fibres come apart, then lift them from a vat on a fine screen.
The fibre matters. Kozo, used for Japanese washi, is about ten millimetres long. Eucalyptus, in most copy paper, is under one.
Paper began in China, earlier than the usual date of a hundred and five. Fragments survive from the first century before the common era.
It reached Baghdad by seven ninety-four, Spain by ten fifty-six, and Fabriano in Italy, where watermarks began in twelve eighty-two.
In nineteen-oh-one, about seventy thousand Japanese households made washi. By two thousand and nine, two hundred and ninety-five remained.
Meanwhile the world makes more paper than ever: about four hundred million tonnes a year.
Hold a sheet under low, raking light, and its surface appears: fine laid lines from the mould's wires, and heavier chain lines.
Ink tells the rest. On unsized paper it blooms into a cloud. Sized with glue, it stays where the brush left it.
On a screen, we rebuild that surface from noise: layers of it, lit from a low angle, until it reads as paper.
Every sheet keeps a record of its fibre, its mould, and the hands that made it.
